patient.chief_complaint: Progressive personality change, behavioral disinhibition, impaired judgment — 20 months; referred by psychiatrist after inadequate response and concern about organic process
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. A is a 48-year-old senior partner at an accounting firm who is referred to the cognitive neurology clinic by her psychiatrist, who notes: 'I have been treating her for 5 months for presumed new-onset mood instability but I am concerned this is not a primary psychiatric condition.' Her husband of 22 years is the primary historian and describes a 20-month history of progressive changes that have been devastating to their family and her career. She has no prior psychiatric history. Approximately 20 months ago, her husband began noticing changes in her behavior at work events — she would make strikingly blunt and sometimes offensive comments about colleagues' appearance or personal choices, then appear confused by others' reactions. She began sending repetitive emails — exact duplicate messages to the same recipients, unaware that she had already sent them. Her work performance declined: she made a significant error on a large audit, which she denied for weeks despite clear documentation. She was placed on administrative leave 4 months ago following a formal complaint by a junior colleague about inappropriate behavior at a work event. She then signed multiple real estate purchase contracts in a 2-week period totaling approximately $850,000 — a completely uncharacteristic impulse for a person her husband describes as 'the most financially conservative person I've ever known.' She proposed that the family move to three different cities simultaneously. She has become fixated on rearranging furniture in the house, doing so multiple times per week. She has developed what her husband calls 'rules' about household objects — their positions, colors, specific arrangements that must not be disturbed. She has completely stopped reading novels, a lifelong passion. She shows no empathy for family members, including their teenage daughter who has been deeply distressed by the changes. The psychiatrist's diagnosis of 'mood instability' led to quetiapine 25 mg, which has had no effect on behaviors. She does not feel depressed. PHQ-9 score is 4 (minimal). The combination of NEW-ONSET behavioral syndrome in a previously psychiatrically healthy 48-year-old, anosognosia, financial disinhibition, perseverative behaviors, and loss of empathy is a classic early bvFTD presentation that requires urgent neuroimaging and biomarker evaluation. The young age makes the diagnosis less expected and increases the likelihood of an identifiable genetic cause.

interactions: Quetiapine in bvFTD: low-dose quetiapine (25 mg) does not significantly improve bvFTD behavioral symptoms and may cause metabolic side effects (glucose, lipids) and sedation
contraindications: Cholinesterase inhibitors — absolutely contraindicated in FTD
warnings: Quetiapine 25 mg at bedtime is commonly used for agitation/behavioral disturbance in FTD — low dose is relatively acceptable but has not been shown to improve FTD-specific symptoms
Metabolic monitoring required with any antipsychotic: glucose, lipids, weight — borderline glucose and LDL may represent quetiapine metabolic effect
Consider tapering quetiapine if behavioral symptoms do not respond — reassess after tapering
Low-dose SSRI (sertraline 50-100 mg) may be more appropriate for bvFTD behavioral symptoms (disinhibition, perseveration)
output.formulary_status: No disease-modifying therapy; GRN-targeted therapy in trials

output.query: bvFTD financial decision-making capacity early onset urgent assessment

results.title: Financial capacity in bvFTD: orbitofrontal disinhibition and financial exploitation risk

output.summary: Financial disinhibition is a cardinal feature of bvFTD, mediated by orbitofrontal cortex dysfunction. bvFTD patients frequently make catastrophic financial decisions — large impulsive purchases, signing contracts, making donations, being susceptible to financial exploitation. Formal financial capacity assessment is indicated when orbitofrontal dysfunction is suspected; cognitive neurology guidelines recommend capacity evaluation and advance planning early in the disease course. Financial exploitation by third parties is a significant risk in bvFTD patients. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia — GRN c.1477C>T pathogenic nonsense variant — young onset age 48 — presenting with minimal MRI changes; previously misdiagnosed as new-onset psychiatric disorder

differential.key_features: No psychiatric history; PHQ-9 4 (no depression); anosognosia; perseverative stereotyped behaviors; frontal FDG-PET hypometabolism; GRN genetic confirmation — no psychiatric disorder causes neurodegenerative biomarkers or frontotemporal hypometabolism

Serum anti-NMDA, anti-LGI1, anti-CASPR2 negative; 20-month progressive course without relapse (autoimmune encephalitis is typically subacute and fluctuating); no seizures or movement disorders; MRI normal (NMDA encephalitis often shows T2/FLAIR changes)
Amyloid PET negative; no hippocampal atrophy; FDG-PET frontal without posterior cingulate sign; behavioral disinhibition profile is FTD not AD
Normal ceruloplasmin; no Kayser-Fleischer rings; age 48 is beyond typical Wilson disease onset (usually <40); normal copper

critical_actions: Young-onset behavioral syndrome (<60 years) with no psychiatric history MUST have full FTD workup — do not diagnose as primary psychiatric disorder without neuroimaging
Financial capacity assessment is URGENT — patient has already signed $850,000 in contracts; impaired financial decision-making is a medical-legal emergency in bvFTD
Genetic testing in young-onset bvFTD has >50% yield for identifiable genetic cause
Autoimmune encephalitis panel must be sent in young patients with behavioral syndrome — treatable if caught early
contraindicated_actions: Stopping workup after minimal MRI — this is the primary diagnostic error; FDG-PET must follow
Prescribing high-dose antipsychotics for behavioral control without FTD workup
key_reasoning_points: Young-onset bvFTD (<60 years) has much higher genetic yield than late-onset — genetic testing is mandatory, not optional, in young-onset cases
AUTOIMMUNE ENCEPHALITIS must be actively excluded in young patients with new behavioral syndrome — anti-NMDA receptor, LGI1, CASPR2 encephalitis can mimic early bvFTD and are TREATABLE

Financial disinhibition leading to large unauthorized purchases or contracts is a medical-legal emergency in bvFTD — formal capacity assessment and power of attorney planning must be initiated urgently

Minimal MRI with abnormal FDG-PET is the characteristic pattern of GRN-FTD (as well as C9orf72) — when behavioral syndrome is present and MRI is minimal, FDG-PET must be performed before concluding no organic disease

red_herrings.intended_effect: Focus on metabolic side effects of quetiapine rather than underlying FTD
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Borderline metabolic findings represent quetiapine side effects; they do not explain the behavioral syndrome and should not distract from the FTD workup
ANA 1:40 is a common non-specific finding in the general population; not indicative of NPSLE or autoimmune encephalitis; full neuropsychiatric lupus workup is not needed

red_herrings.intended_effect: Consider the syndrome unlikely to be genetic FTD without family history
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: GRN mutations can be de novo or have reduced penetrance in prior generations; young onset bvFTD with no family history still requires genetic panel — the GRN pathogenic variant was found despite negative family history

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle bvFTD — GRN pathogenic variant in 48-year-old with minimal MRI and no family history. Key teaching: young-onset behavioral syndrome requires genetic testing and autoimmune exclusion; financial disinhibition is a medical-legal emergency; minimal MRI does not exclude FTD.
